title: Vancouver cop tells inquest she shot Michael Vann Hubbard 'to stop the threat'
article: A Vancouver police officer said she shot knife-wielding Michael Vann Hubbard "to stop the threat" he posed to her and her partner.
"I felt unless I do something about the situation, he would seriously hurt me or cause death," Const. Estilize Wicks testified Monday morning at a coroner's inquest.

Hubbard, 58, died in March 2009 after being shot by Wicks in downtown Vancouver during a confrontation. Wicks and her partner, Const. Celia Tisdall, had responded to a call about a theft from a car around 10:30 a.m. on March 20, 2009.
They headed toward a nearby halfway house, Belkin House, in the 500-block Homer Street, in search of a suspect.
"It's a popular place for us to go to look for suspects," Wicks said.
On the street they spotted Hubbard rifling through a black backpack that matched the description of the stolen bag.
The two officers stopped to talk to Hubbard.

Tisdall testified that when she identified herself and asked Hubbard for his identification and to look in the bag, he reacted "strangely," asking for her PC number. She thought "something was off with this guy or he just hates police."
Tisdall said she told Hubbard she would put him in handcuffs if he didn't comply.
"He got this really weird look on his face. It made the hair on the back of my neck stand up," Tisdall said.
Hubbard then reached behind him and pulled out a utility knife, Tisdall said.
"I was completely shocked."
Tisdall said she drew her firearm and backed up, then called for help. Wicks, who had been observing the situation, also drew her gun and backed away.
"It took me by surprise," Wicks said.
Tisdall said Hubbard screamed obscenities at her and Wicks, telling them to shoot him, while brandishing the knife.
Tisdall said she repeatedly asked Hubbard to drop the knife, but he advanced toward them.
"His eyes were completely wild," Tisdall said.
Tisdall said she was prepared to shoot Hubbard, but he briefly stopped advancing.
Wicks said she then noticed a change in Hubbard's behaviour - he gave her "the 1,000-yard stare.
"He was looking right through me," she said, adding that Hubbard looked angry.
Hubbard then raised the knife and moved toward her, Wicks said.
She aimed at Hubbard's body and fired one shot. He fell to the ground.
While Wicks radioed for an ambulance, Tisdall kicked away the utility knife and tried to handcuff Hubbard.
"My hands were shaking," she said.
Hubbard was pronounced dead at the scene by ambulance attendants.
Based on her dealings with Hubbard, Tisdall said she suspected he had mental-health issues. Wicks, however, disagreed.
"He did not display any overt signs of mental illness," Wicks said.
Both officers have completed a crisis intervention course and deal regularly with people who were mentally ill.
Hubbard was homeless and suffered from schizophrenia.
Neither officer was qualified to carry or use a Taser or beanbag gun.
Wicks said she would not have considered a Taser if she had one because the threat was too great - Hubbard was too close.
At the time of the shooting, the officers had no idea Hubbard was wanted on a warrant after missing an immigration hearing; they didn't even know his name.
It turned out Hubbard had not committed the theft from the vehicle.
The inquest continues.
